analysis.one_liner: Requires testing school and day care drinking water for lead, fast notification of results, and grants to replace lead pipes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in June 2017 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to require the EPA to set a lead action level for drinking water in schools and day care facilities, required water utilities to test water at schools considered at risk, and required utilities to tell schools, health agencies, and parents' local governments within five business days when test results hit that level. It also would have created a federal grant program to pay for testing and for replacing lead pipes and plumbing fixtures with lead-free materials. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who attend schools and day care facilities, along with their parents and teachers, gain a guaranteed system of testing, fast notification, and funding to remove lead from drinking water. School districts and state agencies gain grant money to cover the cost of testing and pipe replacement, with no more than 5 percent of grant funds allowed for administrative costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children in schools and day cares

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to write a national drinking water rule for schools and day care facilities with a lead action level of at least 15 parts per billion, the federal trigger level for taking action on lead contamination.

Requires public water systems to sample for lead at schools the EPA identifies as at risk, and to notify the school district, local health agencies, the municipality, and the state within five business days of receiving results at or above the action level — so families and officials learn about contamination quickly instead of months or years later.

Creates an EPA grant program to pay for lead testing in school drinking water and to replace lead pipes, fittings, and fixtures with lead-free materials, capping administrative costs at 5 percent and requiring test results be posted publicly and shared with parent, teacher, and employee organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Public water utilities would bear the cost of sampling and notification, costs that are commonly passed on to water customers. The federal grant program would be a new federal expenditure, and school districts facing extensive lead plumbing would still need remediation beyond what grants cover.

drawbacks.text: The testing, notification, and response duties fall on public water systems, and those costs are typically recovered through water rates, so household water bills could rise to pay for a program addressing contamination that accumulated over decades.

The bill sets the school action level at whatever the EPA sets generally — no more stringent than the existing federal lead trigger — so schools would not be held to a stricter standard than other users, and contamination below the action level would not trigger notification or replacement funding.

Grant funding for testing and pipe replacement would be a new federal spending commitment whose total size the bill does not specify, and old school buildings with lead plumbing throughout could need remediation well beyond what available grants would cover.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is significant: lead in drinking water harms children's development even at low levels, and most schools are not systematically tested today. The costs are real but conventional — utility sampling costs and a federal grant program — and the bill includes guardrails like the 5 percent administrative cap and public posting of results. A fair objection is that the trigger level mirrors the existing EPA standard rather than a school-specific, stricter one. On balance, the benefits to children's health outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in June 2017 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill on June 21, 2017, with Senator Cory Booker as a cosponsor.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works; that referral was the last action of any kind recorded for the bill in the 115th Congress.
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Democrats, and no further action, votes, or committee activity before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public water utilities avoided new mandatory sampling and five-day notification duties for school customers, and school districts avoided any mandate to test or replace lead plumbing; the federal government also avoided the cost of the grant program. Families with children in schools and day cares got no new protection against lead in drinking water.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call to read; the only support on record was Democratic — the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors — and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill would have required utilities to sample school drinking water and notify officials within five business days of concerning results, adding testing and administrative costs typically recovered through water bills. Utilities' interest in avoiding those mandates ran against the public's interest in learning about lead contamination quickly, though utilities are not the source of most school lead problems — old plumbing is.
A national mandate to sample lead at schools and a grant program reimbursing approved testers would have created a large new market for certified lead testing work.

industries.industry: Plumbing manufacturers and pipe replacement contractors
industries.note: Grant funds could be used to replace lead pipes, fittings, and fixtures with lead-free materials, creating remediation work paid for with federal money.

industries.industry: School districts and state education agencies
industries.note: They were the designated grant recipients, able to recover testing costs and pipe replacement expenses, with results they would have had to post publicly.
